div.head: SCENE I.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Sure, my measter won't be worse nor his word, and fail to come back, from Lunnun, to-day?

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: That's what he won't, mother—Feyther be as true as the clock; which, for certain, do go but indifferent, now, seeing it do stand still.

sp.speaker: Farmer Harrowby
sp.p: Woho! gently wi'em! So, there!

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: His voice, Mary! warn't it?

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: I do think so, fegs!—Stay!
Dear! here be a new drove of rare horned cattle coming into the yard.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Nay, then, I'll warrant my old man be among 'em.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: Yes; there be feyther, as sure as two-pence.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Run, Mary! 'tis my measter! run!
If I ben't all of a twitter to see my old John Harrowby again!

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Gently wi'em—So, boys, so!—See 'em well into the yard, Will; and I'll be wi' you, and the rest of the beasts an' bye.—

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Well, mistress!—How am you? Buss?
So—Well, and how am you?

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Purely, John, I thank ye! Well, and how?

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Why, I be come from Lunnun, you see—I warrant, I smell of smoke like the Nag's-head chimney, in the Borough.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: And what be the freshest news stirring up at Lunnun, John?

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Freshest news? Why, hops have a heavy sale; wheat and malting samples command a brisk market; new tick beans am risen two shillings per quarter; and white and grey peas keep up to their prices.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: Dear! how pleasant 'tis to get the news fresh from Lunnun! La! feyther, if you would but one of those days, now, just carry I up to Lunnun, to learn the genteel fashions at Smithfield, and the Borough, and see the modish ladies there a bit!

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: No, no, Mary—bide at farm, and know when you am well. But, mistress, let's hear a little all how and about it, at home.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Why, first and foremost, John, our lodgers be come.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: No? you don't say so?

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: An hour a'ter you left us, feyther.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: The old gentleman, Lieutenant Worthington—

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: And his daughter, Miss Emily;

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: And his sister-in-law, Madame Lucretia Mac Tab;

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: And his old soldiering servant, Corporal Foss.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Whew! fair and softly! One at a time! one at a time!

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: The Lieutenant be a staid-looking gentleman; and Madam Lucretia—

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: She be an old maid, feyther; and as frumpish a toad, as ever—

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Why, your old maids, for the most part, am but a cross-grain'd kind of a cattle— howsomdever, disappointment fours the best of folks.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: But Miss be the prettiest little creature—!

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: And as sweet-temper'd, feyther!

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Be she though?

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: No more pride nor our Curate. She will fetch a walk with I, in the field, as I go a milking; and speak so kind and so soft! and carry my pail, if I would let her; and all with as much descension, and fallibility!

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Bless her heart!

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: “There was a regiment of Irish dragoons,”—

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: What a dickens! be that son Stephen keeping such a clatter?

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Ah! the boy be crazed, I do think, about soldiering, ever since the Lieutenant's servant, Corporal Foss, have discoursed to him, about champaigning.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Soldiering! I'll soldier the dog, an' he doesn't stick to plough, wi' a devil to 'un!

div.stage: Enter Stephen—his hair dress'd like a soldier's; a black stock, short frock, military spatterdashes; and a carter's whip in his hand.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Feyther, you am welcome back to country quarters. Charming weather for the young wheat, feyther.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Why, you booby, who ha' made thee such a baboon?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: A baboon! he! he! This be milentary, feyther.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: The lad's head be crack'd, for certain.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Crack'd! dang me, but it shall be crack'd an' he don't keep to his business.—

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Answer me, you whelp, you! Who have soap'd up and flower'd your numskull after such a fashion?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Lord, feyther, don't be so vicious. Corporal Foss have put I a little upon drill, that be all.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Upon drill! and leave the farm to go to rack and manger?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: No, feyther, no. I minds my work, and learns my exercise, all under one. I practise “make ready, and present,” in our bean-field; and when the Corporal cries “Fire,” I shoots the carion crows, as do the mischief.—See, feyther, Corporal Foss have given I this pair of splatterdashes. He wore 'em when he went to beat the Spaniels, at Giberaltar.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: I'll tell thee what, Stephen—I have a great mind to beat thee worse nor e'er a Spaniel was beat i' the world. I'll tire thee of soldiering, I warrant thee.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: Hush, brother! you'll feare the whole village.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Wauns! let me come at him.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: No, John!

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: Hold, feyther, hold!

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Don't be so hasty, feyther. I minds my business, I tell'ee. I ha' sow'd three acres of barley before breakfast, already.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Well, come; there may be some hope, then, yet. And how did'st sow it, Stephen?

sp.speaker: Stephen
sp.p: I sow'd it to the tune of the Belleisle march. Tol diddle de doll, &c.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: A Plough-boy, wi' his hair dress'd, sowing barley to the tune of the Belleisle march!

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Well, I ha' got the team at door, wi' a load of straw, for Squire Tallyho—Woho! my hearties! I be a coming to you. Feyther, Corporal says, that our foremost horse, Argus, if he warn't blind, would make a genteel Charger.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: O, plague o' the Corporal!

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: 'Twould do your heart good to hear him talk, in our chimney corner, about mowing down men, in the field of slaughter. Well, well, I be a going, feyther.—Woho! old Argus and Jolly there! The Corporal was wounded, feyther, in the left knee, wi' a hand grenadiero—

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Wauns! an' you don't go, I'll—

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Well, well, I be going.
To the right about, feace!
“God save great George our King!”

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: He sha'n't bide on the farm. I'll turn him adrift. I'll—

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: Don't ye, feyther; don't ye be so bent against poor Stephen.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Hoity toity! and you, too! Why, the whole house will be turn'd topsy-turvy.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: No, indeed, feyther. Tho' Stephen be a little upset with the Corporal, nobody shall turn I topsy-turvy, I do assure you, feyther.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: There! if that ben't Miss Emily calling— Now, do, feyther! do forgive brother Stephen! Coming, Miss! Now do ye, feyther! Coming!

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Pretty goings on, truly! Dang it, I wish, somehow, we had'nt let these lodgers into the house;—but 'twill help us out with our rent, and—

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Ah, John Harrowby!

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Why, what now, Deame?

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: By all I can pick out from the Corporal, who do love to gossip over his beer, our money be but in a ticklish way.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Eh! why, how so?

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: A desperate poor family, I fancy.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: What, then, the Lieutenant—

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Have been in the soldiering line, for thirty long years; but an ugly wound in the arm, which he got in the wars, beyond sea, have made him unfit for his work any more, it do seem.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Poor soul!

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: He be now upon half-pay; which be little enow, for so many mouths, in one family.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Poor soul! his landlord, in Lunnun, wrote uncommon well, sure, about his character, and honesty, and so forth.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: True, John; but he could stand it, in Lunnun, no longer, you do see.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Why, look ye, Deame—I didn't, of a certainty, intend to let our best parlours for nothing: but I wish I may be shot if I can give harsh treatment to an honest man, in misfortune, under my thatch; who have wasted his strength, and his youth, in guarding the land which do give us English farmers a livelihood.

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Ah, John! you am at your old kind ways, now!

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Hark! he be opening the parlour door —Leave us together a bit, mistress: I'll speak to 'un, and—

sp.speaker: Dame.
sp.p: Well, I'll go, John—Ah! bless thy good old heart! I do like to do a good turn myself; but, somehow, my old man do always get the start o' me.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: A good day to you, Sir!
You am welcome into Kent, Sir,—to my humble cottage, here.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Oh, my landlord, I suppose—Farmer Harrowby?

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Yes, Sir, I be Farmer Harrowby. I hope all things am to your liking, at Stocks' Green, Sir—I hope the lodgings, Sir, and my wife, have been agreeable to you, Sir, and so forth.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Nothing can be better. You are well situated here, Mr. Harrowby.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: We am all in the rough, Sir; farmer-like —but the place be well enow for poor folk, Sir.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: What does he mean by that?

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: I be content in my station. There be no reason why a poor man should not be happy.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: A million!

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Am there? Well now, I can't see that: for, putting the case, now, Sir, that you was poor, like I—

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I will not suffer you, Sir, to put a case so familiarly curious.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Nay, I meant no offence, I'll be sworn, Sir.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: But, if you wish to know my sentiments, as far as it may concern yourself, in any money transactions between us, be assured of this:—I have too nice a sense of a gentleman's dignity, and too strong a feeling for a poor man's necessity, to permit him to wait a day for a single shilling, which I am indebted to him.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Dang it! he must be poor; for your great gentry, now-a-days, do pay in a clean contrary fashion.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I shall settle with you, for the lodgings, Mr. Harrowby, weekly—One week is due to-day, and—

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: No, Sir, no—under favour, I would like it best quarterly—or half-yearly—or at any long time may suit your conveni—I mean, may suit your pleasure, Sir.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Why so?

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Because—humph—because, Sir—pray, if I may make so bold, Sir, how often may the pay-days come round, with the army-gentlemen, and such like?

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Insolent! receive your money, Sir, and let me pass from your apartment

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Then I wish I may be burnt if I take it now, and that be flat, Sir.

You am a brave, good gentleman, I be told, Sir;—wi a family, and—and—and—in short, there am some little shopmen, of our village, who may press you hard, to settle by the week; pay them greedy ones first, Sir; and if there be enow, at last, left for I, well and good; and if you am inclined for riding, Sir, there be always a gelding at your service, without charge. I be a plain man, Sir; but I do mean nothing but respect; and, so, I humbly with you a good day, Sir.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: How am I mortified! What has this man heard? Yet, this little simple movement of rustick humanity towards me has—Pshaw! where is my fortitude! Inured to the frowns of the world, one kindly smile of compassion subdues me. Is there a state more galling than to need the decent means of maintaining the appearance which liberal birth, education, and profession demand? Yes,— yes, there is an aggravation!—'Tis to have a daughter nursed in her father's afflictions, with little more to share with her than the bread of his anguish, the bitter cup of his sorrows. To see, while I am sinking to my grave, my friendless, motherless child.—Let me draw a veil over this picture —'Twere not philosophy, but brutality, to look upon it unmoved. I can not!

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: —An apartment in Sir Charles Cropland's house; Sir Charles Cropland at breakfast; his Valet de chambre adjusting his hair.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Has old Warner, the steward, been told that I arrived last night?

sp.speaker: Valet.
sp.p: Yes, Sir Charles; with orders to attend you this morning.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: What can a man of fashion do with himself in the country, at this damn'd dull time of the year!

sp.speaker: Valet.
sp.p: It is a very pleasant, to-day, out in the park, Sir Charles.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Pleasant, you booby! How can the country be pleasant in the middle of Spring? All the world's in London.

sp.speaker: Valet.
sp.p: I think, somehow, it looks so lively, Sir Charles, when the corn is coming up.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Blockhead! Vegetation makes the face of a country look frightful. It spoils hunting. Yet, as my business on my estate, here, is to raise supplies for my pleasures elsewhere, my journey is a wise one. What day of the month was it yesterday, when I left town, on this wise expedition?

sp.speaker: Valet.
sp.p: The first of April, Sir Charles.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Umph!—When Mr. Warner comes, shew him in.

sp.speaker: Valet.
sp.p: I shall, Sir Charles.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: This same lumbering timber upon my ground has its merits. Trees are notes, issued from the bank of Nature, and as current as those payable to Abraham Newland. I must get change for a few oaks, for I want cash consumedly. So, Mr. Warner!

sp.speaker: Warner.
sp.p: Your honour is right welcome into Kent. I am proud to see Sir Charles Cropland on his estate again. I hope you mean to stay on the spot for some time, Sir Charles.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: A very tedious time. Three days, Mr. Warner.

sp.speaker: Warner.
sp.p: Ah, good Sir! things wou'd prosper better if you honour'd us with your presence a little more. I wish you lived entirely upon the estate, Sir Charles.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Thank you, Warner;—but modern men of fashion find it devilish difficult to live upon their estates.

sp.speaker: Warner.
sp.p: The country about you so charming!

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Look ye, Warner—I must hunt in Leicestershire—for that's the thing. In the frosts, and the spring months, I must be in town, at the Clubs—for that's the thing.—In summer, I must be at the watering places—for that's the thing. Now, Warner, under these circumstances, how is it possible for me to reside upon my estate? For my estate being in Kent—

sp.speaker: Warner.
sp.p: The most beautiful part of the County.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Curse beauty! we don't mind that in Leicestershire. My estate, I say, being in Kent—

sp.speaker: Warner.
sp.p: A land of milk and honey!—

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: I hate milk and honey.

sp.speaker: Warner.
sp.p: A land of fat!—

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Damn your fat!—listen to me—my estate being in Kent—

sp.speaker: Warner.
sp.p: So woody!

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Curse the wood! No—that's wrong— for it's convenient. I am come on purpose to cut it.

sp.speaker: Warner.
sp.p: Ah! I was afraid so! Dice on the table, and, then, the axe to the root! Money lost at play, and then, good lack! the forest groans for it.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: But you are not the forest, and why the devil do you groan for it?

sp.speaker: Warner.
sp.p: I heartily wish, Sir Charles, you may not encumber the goodly estate. Your worthy ancestors had views for their posterity.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: And I shall have views for my posterity —I shall take special care the trees sha'n't intercept their prospect.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Mr. Ollapod, the apothecary, is in the hall, Sir Charles, to inquire after your health.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Shew him in.

The fellow's a character, and treats time as he does his patients. He shall kill a quarter of an hour for me, this morning. In short, Mr. Warner, I must have three thousand pounds in three days. Fell timber to that amount, immediately. 'Tis my peremptory order, Sir.

sp.speaker: Warner.
sp.p: I shall obey you, Sir Charles; but 'tis with a heavy heart! Forgive an old servant of the family, if he grieves to see you forget some of the duties for which society has a claim upon you.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: What do you mean by duties?

sp.speaker: Warner.
sp.p: Duties, Sir Charles, which the extravagant man of property can never fulfil—Such as to support the dignity of an English landholder, for the honour of old England; to promote the welfare of his honest tenants; and to succour the industrious poor, who naturally look up to him for assistance. But I shall obey you, Sir Charles.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: A tiresome old blockhead! But where is this Ollapod? His jumble of physick and shooting may enliven me—And, to a man of gallantry, in the country, his intelligence is, by no means, uninteresting, nor his services inconvenient. Ha! Ollapod!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Sir Charles, I have the honour to be your slave. Hope our health is good. Been a hard winter here—Sore throats were plenty; so were woodcocks. Flush'd four couple, one morning, in a half-mile walk, from our town, to cure Mrs. Quarles of a quinsey. May coming on soon, Sir Charles—season of delight, love, and campaigning! Hope you come to sojourn, Sir Charles. Shouldn't be always on the wing—that's being too flighty. He, he, he! Do you take, good Sir, do you take?

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Oh, yes, I take. But, by the cockade in your hat, Ollapod, you have added lately, it seems, to your avocations.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: He! he! yes, Sir Charles. I have, now, the honour to be Cornet in the Volunteer Association Corps, of our town. It fell out unexpected—pop, on a sudden; like the going off of a field-piece, or an alderman in an apoplexy.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Explain.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Happening to be at home—rainy day— no going out to sport, blister, shoot, nor bleed— was busy behind the counter—You know my shop, Sir Charles—Galen's head over the door—new-gilt him last week, by the bye—looks as fresh as a pill.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Well, no more on that head now— Proceed.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: On that Head! he! he! he! That's very well; very well, indeed! Thank you, good Sir, I owe you one.—Churchwarden Posh, of our town, being ill of an indigestion, from eating three pounds of measly pork, at a Vestry dinner, I was making up a cathartick for the patient; when, who should strut into the shop, but Lieutenant Grains, the Brewer —sleek as a dray-horse—in a smart scarlet jacket, tastily turn'd up with a rhubarb-colour'd lapelle. I confess his figure struck me. I look'd at him, as I was thumping the mortar, and felt instantly inoculated with a military ardour.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Inoculated! I hope your ardour was of a favourable sort.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Ha! ha! That's very well—very well, indeed!—Thank you, good Sir, I owe you one. We first talk'd of shooting—He knew my celebrity that way, Sir Charles. I told him, the day before, I had kill'd six brace of birds—I thumpt on at the mortar—We then talk'd of physick—I told him, the day before, I had kill'd—lost, I mean,—six brace of patients—I thumpt on at the mortar—eyeing him all the while; for he look'd devilish flashy, to be sure; and I felt an itching to belong to the Corps. The medical, and military, both deal in death, you know—so, 'twas natural. He! he!—Do you take, good Sir? do you take?

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Take? Oh, nobody can miss.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: He then talk'd of the Corps itself: said it was sickly; and if a professional person would administer to the health of the Association—dose the men, and drench the horse—he could, perhaps, procure him a Cornetcy.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Well, you jump'd at the offer?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Jump'd! I jump'd over the counter— kick'd down Churchwarden Posh's cathartick, into the pocket of Lieutenant Grains's smart scarlet jacket, tastily turn'd up with a rhubarb-colour'd lapelle; embraced him and his offer; and I am now Cornet Ollapod, apothecary, at the Galen's head, of the Association Corps of Cavalry, at your service.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: I wish you joy of your appointment. You may now distil water for the shop, from the laurels you gather in the field.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Water for—Oh! laurel water—he! he! Come, that's very well—very well indeed! Thank you, good Sir, I owe you one. Why, I fancy fame will follow, when the poison of a small mistake I made has ceased to operate.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: A mistake?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Having to attend Lady Kitty Carbuncle, on a grand field-day, I clapt a pint bottle of her Ladyship's diet-drink into one of my holsters; intending to proceed to the patient, after the exercise was over—I reach'd the martial ground, and jallop'd —gallop'd, I mean—wheel'd, and flourish'd, with great eclât; but when the word “Fire” was given, meaning to pull out my pistol, in a hell of a hurry, I presented, neck foremost, the damn'd diet-drink of Lady Kitty Carbuncle; and the medicine being, unfortunately, fermented, by the jolting of my horse, it forced out the cork, with a prodigious pop, full in the face of my gallant commander.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: But, in the midst of so many persuits, how proceeds practice among the ladies?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: He! he! I should be sorry not to feel the pulse of a pretty woman, now and then, Sir Charles. Do you take, good Sir, do you take?

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Any new faces, since I left the country?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Nothing worth an item—Nothing new arrived in our town. In the village, to be sure, hard by, a most brilliant beauty has lately given lustre to the lodgings of Farmer Harrowby.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Indeed! is she come-at-able, Ollapod?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Oh no! Full of honour as a Corps of Cavalry; tho', plump as a partridge, and mild as emulsion. Miss Emily Worthington, I may venture to say—

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Hey? who? Emily Worthington!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: With her father—

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: An old officer in the army?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: The same.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: And a stiff maiden aunt?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Stiff as a ram-rod.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Tol de rol lol!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Bless me! he is seized with St. Vitus's dance.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: 'Tis she, by Jupiter! my dear Ollapod!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Oh, my dear Sir Charles!

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: The very girl who has just slipt thro' my fingers, in London.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Oho!

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: You can serve me materially, Ollapod. I know your good nature, in a case like this, and—

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: State the symptoms of the case, Sir Charles.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Oh, common enough. Saw her in London by accident: wheedled the old maiden aunt; kept out of the father's way; follow'd Emily more than a month, without success;—and, eight days ago she vanished—there's the outline.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: I see no matrimonial symptoms in our case, Sir Charles.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: 'Sdeath! do you think me mad? But, introduce yourself to the family, and pave the way for me. Come mount your horse—I'll explain more, as you go to the stable:—but I am in a flame, in a fever, till I hear further.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: In a fever! I'll send you physick enough to fill a baggage-waggon.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: So! a long bill as the price of his politeness!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: You need not bleed; but you must have medicine.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: If I must have medicine, Ollapod, I fancy I shall bleed pretty freely.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: He! he! Come, that's very well! very well indeed! Thank you, good Sir, I owe you one. Before dinner, a strong dose of coloquintida, senna, scammony, and gambouge;—

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Oh, damn scammony and gambouge!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: At night a narcotick;—next day, saline draughts, camphorated julep, and—

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Zounds! only go, and I'll swallow your whole shop.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Galen forbid! 'Tis enough to kill every customer I have in the parish!—Then we'll throw in the bark—by the bye, talking of bark, Sir Charles, that Juno of yours is the prettiest pointer bitch—

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Well, well, she is yours.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: My dear Sir Charles! such sport, next shooting season!—If I had but a double barrell'd gun—

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Take mine that hangs in the hall.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: My dear Sir Charles!—Here's a morning's work! senna and coloquintida—

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Well, be gone then.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: I'm off—! Scammony and gambouge—

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Nay, fly, man!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: I do, Sir Charles—A double barrell'd gun—I fly—the bark—I'm going—Juno, the bitch—a narcotick—

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Oh, the devil!

div.head: SCENE I.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: We am not discoursing about your master's bravery, nor his ableness, Mr. Corporal; it be about his goodness, and that like.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: A good officer, do you see, can't help being a kind-hearted man; for one of his foremost duties tells him to study the comfort of the poor people below him.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Dang it, that be the duty of our church-wardens; but many poor people do complain of 'em.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: An officer, Mr. Harrowby, is n't a bit like a churchwarden. Ship off an officer, we'll say, with his company, to a foreign climate. He lands, and endures heat, cold, fatigue, hunger, thirst, sickness—Now marching over the burning plain— now up to his knees in wet, in the trench—Now— damn it, Farmer, how can a man suffer such hardships, with a parcel of honest fellows, under his command, and not learn to feel for his fellow-creatures?

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Well; and that be true, sure! And have your master, Lieutenant Worthington, learnt this?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: His honour was beloved by the whole regiment. When his wife was shot in his arms, as she lay in his tent—there was n't a dry eye in our corps.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Shot in his arms! And, was she, though?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: I never like to think on't, because— Pshaw!
I hate to be unsoldier-like —I whimper'd enough, about it, seventeen years ago.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Nay, take no shame, Mr. Corporal, take no shame. Honest tears, upon honest faces, am, for all the world, like growing showers, upon my meadows—the wet do raise their value.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: However, he had something left to console him, after her death.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: And what ware that?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: 'Twas his child, Mr. Harrowby. Our Miss Emily was then but three years old. I have heard his honour say, her mother had fled to the abode of peace, and left her innocent in the lap of war.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Pretty soul! she must have been quite scared and frightful.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: She didn't know her danger. She little thought, then, that a chance ball might take her father too—and leave her a helpless orphan, in a strange country.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: And, if it had so fell out?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Why, then, perhaps, nothing would have been left her but a poor Corporal, to buckle her on his knapsack: but I would have struggled hard with fortune, to rake up a little pittance for the child of a kind master; whom I had follow'd thro' many a campaign, and seen fight his first battle, and his last.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Do, give us your hand, Mr. Corporal. I'll be shot, now, if I could see an old soldier travelling by, wi' his knapsack, loaded in that manner, and not call him in, to cheer the poor soul, on his journey.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: I thank you very kindly, Mr. Harrowby;— but Providence order'd things otherwise: for on the thirteenth of September, in the year eighty-two, a few months after my poor mistress's death, the bursting of a shell, in the garrison, crush'd his honour's arm almost to shivers; and I got wounded on the cap of my knee here. It disabled us, both, from ever serving again.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: That turn'd out but a baddish day's work, Mr. Corporal.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: It turn'd out one of the best day's work, for an Englishman, that ever was seen, Mr. Harrowby; for on that day, our brave General Elliot gave the Frenchmen, and Spaniards, as hearty a drubbing, at Gibraltar, as ever they had in their lives. A true soldier, Mr. Harrowby, would part with all his limbs, and his life after them, rather than Old England should have lost the glory of that day.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: And how long, now, might you lay in your wounds and torments, Mr. Corporal?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: 'Twas some time before either of us could be moved: and when we could—being unfit for duty any longer—I follow'd his honour, with little Miss Emily, into America, where the war was newly finish'd; for things are cheap there, Mr. Harrowby, and that best suits a Lieutenant's pocket.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: I do fear it do indeed, Mr. Corporal.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: But we had a pretty cottage in Canada, on the banks of the river St. Lawrence; shut out from all the world, as I may say.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Desperate lonesome sure, for soldiers, who am used to be in a bustle.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Why, we soon grew used to it, Mr. Harrowby; and should never have left it, perhaps, if something hadn't called his honour, a year ago, into England.

sp.speaker: Farmer.
sp.p: Well, I must away about the farm— And, do tell your master, Mr. Corporal—tell him gently though, for he be a little touchy-like, I do see—that if so be things am cheap in America, they mayn't be found a morsel dearer here, when a wounded English soldier do sit at the door of an English farmer.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: —If you am exposed to drill I a bit, Corporal, now be your time.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: You are back early to-day, my honest lad.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Yes; I do love to be betimes at parade. You'll never find I last comer, when men am to be mustarded! I ha' finished my day's work, outright.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: You have lost no time, then.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: No—I ha' lost a cart and horses.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Lost a cart and horses!

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Aye, as good;—for as I ware a coming back, empty-handed, wi' our cart, I thought I might as well practise a little, as I walk'd by the side on't —so I held up my head—in the milentary fashion, you do know—and began a marching near foot foremost, to the tune of the British Grenadiers.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Dang it! while I ware a carrying my head up, as straight as a hop-pole, our leading horse, blind Argus, drags lean Jolly, wi' the cart at his tail, into a slough.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Zounds! so you plunged the baggage into a morass?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: I don't know what you do call a morass; but they am sticking up to their necks, in the mud, at the bottom of Waggon-lodge field.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: O fie! you should have look'd to them better.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Look'd to 'em! Why, how could that possible be, mun? when you teach'd I to hold up my nose to the clouds, like a pig in the wind.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Here,—Juno! Juno! Put my pointer into your stable, my lad.—Thank ye— if ever you're ill, I'll physick you for nothing.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Oh, that be Mr. Ollapod, the pottercarrier.

div.stage: Enter Ollapod, with a double-barrell'd gun.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Stephen, how's your health? Fine weather for the farmers.—Corporal, I've heard of you;— charming Spring for campaigning!—I am Cornet Ollapod, of the Galen's head; come to pay my respects to your family. Stephen, how's your father, and his hogs, geese, daughter, wife, bullocks, and so forth? Are the partridges beginning to lay yet, Stephen?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Am you come to shoot the young birds, before they am hatch'd, wi' that double-barrell'd gun, Mr. Ollapod?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Come, that's very well! very well indeed for a bumpkin! Thank you, good Stephen, I owe you half a one. I hope your master, Lieutenant Worthington's well,—whose acquaintance I covet. We soldiers mix together as naturally as medicine in a mortar.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Is your Honour in the army then?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: He be only a Coronet, in the town corpse.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: I wish that lout had a lock'd jaw! Our Association is as fine, and, I may say, without vanity, will be as healthy a Corps, when their spring physick is finish'd, as any regular regiment in England.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Why, your honour, I have seen a good deal of service in the regular way; and know nothing about Associations; but I think, an' please your honour, if men take up arms to defend their country, they deserve to be thank'd, and respected for it, and it doesn't signify a brass farthing what they are called.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Right—the name's nothing—merit's all— Rhubarb's rhubarb, call it what you will.—Do you take, Corporal? do you take?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: I never took any in all my life, an please your Honour.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: That's very well, very well indeed! Thank you, corporal—I owe you one—Now, introduce me to the family.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: I can't without orders; and his Honour is walk'd out.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: That's right; exercise is conducive to health. I'll walk in.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Under favour, your honour, I stand centinel here; and I can't let a stranger pass, without consulting the garrison. If you'll please to saunter about, for half an hour, I shall speak to our ladies, and—

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Well, do so—Stephen, come with me about the grounds.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: I don't like to march wi' you, Mr. Ollapod —You am no regular—Dang me, if I budge wi' him, Corporal, without your word of command.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: But, damn it, I'm of the Cavalry.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: No matter for that. You am upon our ground, and unhorsed—Now, Corporal—!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Well, if I must, I—

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: March!

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Come, pottercarrier. Tol de rol.

div.stage: [Exeunt. Stephen and Ollapod at the side. The Corporal into the house.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Miss Lucretia MacTab, and Emily Worthington discover'd, at a table. On the table are work-boxes, pens, ink, and paper, &c.—Emily at work, Lucretia looking over a shabby memorandum-book.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Miss Emily Worthington, you have work'd those flowers most miserably, child.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Dear, now, I am very sorry for that. I was in hopes they might have sold for something, at London, that I might have surprised my father with the money.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Sold! Ah, you have none of the proper pride which my side of the family should have given you—But, let me look over my expences since we have been here.

“To one week's washing, and darning, for the Honourable Miss Lucretia MacTab, one and sevenpence.”—By the bye, Miss Emily, that sprig of myrtle is thicker than a birch-broom, and the white rose looks just like a powder-puff.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Indeed, I copied them from nature, grand aunt.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Grand aunt! you know I hate that hideous title: but 'tis the fault of your wild American education.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Nay, there can be no fault in that; for my dear father educated me himself, in our little cottage, in Canada.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: He might have taught you, then, a little more respect for me, who am of the elevated part of the family—“Snuff from the chandler, a half-penny,”
—You know, child, I am your relation, on your deceased mother's side, and of the noble blood of the MacTabs.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Yes, I know that now: but my poor mother had no relation on her side, when her father, Lord Lofty, abandon'd her for marrying.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: My brother, Lord Lofty, acted as became his rank. You will please to recollect he was one of the oldest barons in Scotland.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Was he, indeed! And you were born only three years after him, grand aunt!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Miss Emily, your ignorance is greater than—
I meant, his title is one of the most ancient of the Barony; and he might well be offended at the marriage of my deceased niece, his daughter; for, you know, your father is a mere —but, no matter.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Indeed, but it does matter, though. My father is a gentleman by birth, education, and manners; and that's a character as well deserving respect as the proudest Peer of the realm.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: And, pray, what have I insinuated against your father? On the contrary, you might remember how handsomely I have offer'd him my countenance.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: I remember it was a year ago that you came, and said you would live with us;—when your brother, Lord Lofty, died so much in debt, and left you destitute.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: More shame for him! But, didn't I, then, affectionately fly to your father, and tell him I wou'd allow him the honour to maintain me for the future? And hav'n't I, notwithstanding his obscure situation, and narrow finances, kindly lived at the Lieutenant's charge, in the most condescending way in the world?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Condescending!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Yes, Miss Emily; but, it seems, by forgetting me, you forget yourself.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: No—indeed I know my situation. I am a poor Officer's child: born in the seat of war; rear'd, afterwards, in the wilds of America—rear'd by a kind father, with more cost than his poverty could well bestow. He has dropt, in our retreat, many and many a tear of affection on me; and, as often as I have seen him mourn my mother's loss, I have wonder'd to think that her father, in splendour, could be so hard-hearted, while mine, in poverty, was so kind!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Still on the cruelty of your mother's relations! But, would you be guided by me, Miss Emily, I wou'd make your fortune. Had you follow'd my opinion, before we left town, relative to Sir Charles Cropland, as a husband.—

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Oh, pray don't mention his name.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: And, why not, Miss Emily?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Because I'm sure he is a libertine.—The familiar looks he gave me—

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Looks! psha! Sir Charles's are the manners, child, of our young men of high fashion.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: 'Tis a great pity, then, our young men of high fashion have so insulting a way of noticing lowly virtue. A coxcomb that stares humble modesty out of countenance, must be a very cruel coxcomb; and 'tis a sad thing for the heart to be unfeeling when the head is empty!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Ha! another of your Canada crotchets— hatch'd on the banks of St. Lawrence; where solitude sits brooding on romance. But will you follow my counsel?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: In respect to Sir Charles Cropland? No —never. You received his visits without my father's knowledge. I would not wed the worthiest man without his consent; and he would not command me to marry the wealthiest, whom I could not esteem.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Pshaw! your father's doctrines, child, have made him a beggar.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: A beggar! no, madam, he is rich enough to shelter you, who asperse him.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Shelter! shelter, indeed, to a MacTab, who affords him her countenance! I shall acquaint your father, Miss Emily, with your rudeness to me.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Acquaint him with all, madam.—Tell him, when his daughter hears him misrepresented by—Tell him—You break my heart, madam—Tell him what you please.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: I am come, an' please you, with intelligence of—What! is my young lady a crying?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Deliver your message, fellow, and ask no questions.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: An please your ladyship's honour, when an old soldier sees a woman in distress, 'tis to be hoped he may take just half a moment to give her some comfort. Miss Emily!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Blockhead! what excuse has a soldier for half a moment's delay in his business?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: The best excuse, an please you, may be half a moment's charity. A kind commander is loth to punish a poor fellow for doing what heaven rewards. What's the matter, Miss Emily?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: 'Tis nothing, good Corporal—lead me to the door of my chamber.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: You may be taught your duty to me better, sir.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: I humbly beg pardon; but my first duty, in these quarters, is to my master, and his child; I know that as a servant. My second is, to a woman in grief;—I am sure of that as a man. My third is to your ladyship's honour; and I'll be back to perform it, in as quick a march as a cripple can make of it. Come, Miss Emily, come!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Provoking! a stupid, technical, old— But what can a woman of birth expect—when the ducks waddle into her drawing-room, and her groom of the chambers is a lame soldier of foot!

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: There is one Mr. Ollapod at the gate, an' please your ladyship's honour, come to pay a visit to the family.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Ollapod? What is the gentleman?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: He says he's a Cornet in the Galen's head. 'Tis the first time I ever heard of the Corps.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Ha,—some new-raised regiment. Shew the gentleman in.

The country, then, has heard of my arrival, at last. A woman of condition, in a family, can never long conceal her retreat. Ollapod! that sounds like an ancient name. If I am not mistaken, he is nobly descended.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Madam, I have the honour of paying my respects. Sweet spot, here, among the cows;— good for consumptions—Charming woods hereabouts —Pheasants flourish—so do agues—Sorry not to see the good Lieutenant—admire his room, hope, soon, to have his company. Do you take, good madam, do you take?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I beg, Sir, you will be seated.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Oh, dear madam!
A charming chair to bleed in!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I am sorry Mr. Worthington is not at home, to receive you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: You are a relation of the Lieutenant, madam?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I! only by his marriage, I assure you, Sir. Aunt to his deceased wife: but I am not surprised at your question. My friends, in town, would wonder to see the Honourable Miss Lucretia MacTab, sister to the late Lord Lofty, cooped up in a farm house.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: The Honourable! humph! a bit of quality tumbled into decay—The sister of a dead Peer in a pig-stye!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: You are of the military, I am inform'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: He! he! yes, madam. Cornet Ollapod, of our Volunteers—a fine healthy troop—ready to give the enemy a dose, whenever they dare to attack us.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I was always prodigiously partial to the military. My great grandfather, Marmaduke, Baron Lofty, commanded a troop of horse, under the Duke of Marlborough; that famous general of his age.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Marlborough was a hero of a man, madam; and lived at Woodstock—a sweet sporting country; where Rosamond perish'd by poison— Arsenick, as likely as any thing.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: And have you served much, Mr. Ollapod?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: He! he! Yes, Madam—served all the nobility, and gentry, for five miles round.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Sir!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: And shall be happy to serve the good Lieutenant, and his family.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: We shall be proud of your acquaintance, Sir. A gentleman of the Army is always an acquisition, among the Goths and Vandals of the country; where every sheepish Squire has the air of an apothecary.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Madam! An apothe—Zouns!—hum! —He! he! I—You must know, I—I deal a little in Galenicals, myself

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Galenicals! Oh, they are for operations, I suppose, among the military.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Operations! He! he! Come, that's very well, very well indeed! Thank you, good Madam, I owe you one. Galenicals, Madam, are medicines.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Medicines!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Yes, physick: buckthorn, senna, and so forth.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Why, then, you are an apothecary!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: And man-midwife, at your service, Madam.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: At my service, indeed!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Yes, Madam! Cornet Ollapod, at the gilt Galen's head, of the volunteer Association Corps of Cavalry—As ready for the foe, as a customer: always willing to charge them both—Do you take, good Madam, do you take?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: And has the Honourable Miss Lucretia MacTab been talking, all this while, to a petty dealer in drugs?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Drugs! dam'me, she turns up her honourable nose, as if she was going to swallow them! No man more respected than myself, Madam. Courted by the Corps, idolized by invalids; and for a shot—ask my friend, Sir Charles Cropland.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Is Sir Charles Cropland a friend of yours, Sir?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Intimate. He doesn't make wry faces at physick, whatever others may do, Madam. This village flanks the intrenchments of his park—full of fine fat venison; which is as light a food for digestion as—.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: But he is never on his estate here, I am told.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: He quarters there at this moment.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Bless me!—Has Sir Charles, then—?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Told me all—your accidental meeting in the metropolis, and his visits when the Lieutenant was out.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Oh, shocking! I declare I shall faint.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Faint! never mind that, with a medical man in the room—I can bring you about, in a twinkling.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: And, what has Sir Charles Cropland presumed to advance about me?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Oh, nothing derogatory. Respectful as a duck-legg'd drummer to a commander in chief.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I have only proceeded, in this affair, from the purest motives; and in a mode becoming a MacTab.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: None dare to doubt it.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: And, if Sir Charles has dropt in, to a dish of tea, with myself and Emily, in London, when the Lieutenant was out, I see no harm in it.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Nor I, neither:—except that tea shakes the nervous system to shatters. But, to the point; the Baronet's my bosom friend—Having heard you were here, “Ollapod,” says he, squeezing my hand in his own, which had strong symptoms of fever, “Ollapod,” says he, “you are a military man, and may be trusted.”—“I'm a Cornet,” says I, “and close as a pill-box”—“Fly, then, to Miss Lucretia MacTab, that honourable picture of prudence”—

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: He! he! did Sir Charles say that?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: How these tabbies love to be toaded!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: In short, Sir Charles, I perceive, has appointed you his emissary; to consult with me, when he may have an interview.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Madam, you are the sharpest shot at the truth I ever met in my life. And, now we are in consultation, what think you of a walk with Miss Emily, by the old elms, at the back of the village, this evening?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Why, I am willing to take any steps which may promote Emily's future welfare.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Take steps! what, in a walk? He! he! come, that's very well, very well indeed! Thank you, good Madam; I owe you one. I shall communicate to my friend, with due despatch. Command Cornet Ollapod, on all occasions; and whatever the gilt Galen's-head can produce—

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Oh, Sir!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: By the bye, I have some double distill'd lavender water, much admired in our Corps. Permit me to send a pint bottle, by way of present.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Dear Sir, I shall rob you.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Quite the contrary:—For I'll set it down to Sir Charles as a quart.
Madam, your slave. You have prescribed for our patient like an able physician.—Not a step.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Nay, I insist—

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Then I must follow in the rear. The physician always before the apothecary.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Apothecary! Sir, in this business, I look upon you as a general officer.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Do you? Thank you, good Ma'am: I owe you one.

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: —An apartment in Sir Robert Bramble's house.
Sir Robert Bramble, and Humphrey Dobbins.

sp.speaker: Sir Robert.
sp.p: I tell you what, Humphrey Dobbins; there isn't a syllable of sense in all you have been saying. But, I suppose you will maintain that there is.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Yes! is that the way you talk to me, you old boar? What's my name?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Robert Bramble.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: A'n't I a Baronet? Sir Robert Bramble, of Blackberry Hall, in the county of Kent? 'Tis time you should know it; for you have been my clumsy, two fisted valet de chambre, these thirty years—Can you deny that?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Humph!

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Humph! what the devil do you mean by humph? Open the rusty door of your mouth, and make your ugly voice walk out of it. Why don't you answer my question?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Because, if I contradicted you there, I should tell a lie; and, whenever I agree with you, you are sure to fall out.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Humphrey Dobbins—I have been so long endeavouring to beat a few brains into your pate, that all your hair has tumbled off it, before I can carry my point.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: What then? Our Parson says, my head is an emblem of both our honours.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Aye, because honours, like your head, are apt to be empty.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: No;—but if a servant has grown bald under his master's nose, it looks as if there was honesty on one side, and regard for it on t'other.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Why, to be sure, old Humphrey, you are as honest a—. Psha! the parson means to palaver us;—but, to return to my position,— I tell you I don't like your flat contradiction.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Yes, you do.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I tell you I don't. I only love to hear men's arguments, and I hate their flummery.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: What do you call flummery?

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Flattery, you blockhead! A dish too often served up, by paltry poor men, to paltry rich ones.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: I never serve it up to you.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: No, I'll be sworn. You give me a dish of a different description.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Umph! what is it?

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Sour krout, you old crab.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: I have held you a stout tug at argument, this many a year.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: And yet I could never teach you a syllogism. Now, mind; when a poor man assents to what a rich man says, I suspect he means to flatter him. Now I am rich, and hate flattery—Ergo, when a poor man subscribes to my opinion, I hate him.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: That's wrong.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Very well—Negatur. Now prove it.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Put the case so, then—I am a poor man—.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: You lie, you scoundrel! You know you shall never want while I have a shilling.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Bless you!

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Pshaw! proceed.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Well, then, I am a poor—I must be a poor man, now, or I shall never get on.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Well, get on. Be a poor man.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: I am a poor man; and I argue with you, and convince you you are wrong—then you call yourself a blockhead, and I am of your opinion: Now, that's no flattery.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Why, no:—but, when a man's of the same opinion with me, he puts an end to the argument; and that puts an end to conversation:—So, I hate him for that. But where's, my nephew, Frederick?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Been out these two hours.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: An undutiful cub!—Only arrived from Russia last night; and, though I told him to stay at home, till I rose, he's scampering over the fields, like a Calmuc Tartar.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: He's a fine fellow.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: He has a touch of our family. Don't you think he's a little like me, Humphrey?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Bless you, not a bit. You are as ugly an old man as ever I clapt my eyes on.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Now, that's damn'd impudent! But there's no flattery in it; and it keeps up the independence of argument. His father, my brother, Job, is of as tame a spirit! Humphrey, you remember my brother Job?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Yes; you drove him to Russia, five-and-twenty years ago.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I drove him!

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Yes, you did—You wou'd never let him be at peace, in the way of argument.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: At peace! Zounds! he would never go to war.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: He had the merit to be calm.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
Dob.
sp.p: And, the poor meek gentleman went to Russia, for a quiet life.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: A quiet life! Why, he married the moment he got there. Tack'd himself to the shrew relict of a Russian merchant; and continued a speculation with her, in furs, flax, pot-ashes, tallow, linen, and leather. And, what's the consequence? thirteen months ago, he broke.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Poor soul! his wife should have follow'd the business for him.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I fancy she did follow it; for she died just as it went to the devil. And, now, this madcap, Frederick, is sent over to me for protection. Poor Job! now he's in distress, I mustn't neglect his son.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Here comes his son—That's Mr. Frederick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Ah, my dear uncle! good morning. Your park is nothing but beauty.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Who bid you caper over my beauty? I told you to stay in doors, till I got up.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Eh? Egad so you did! I had as intirely forgot it, as—

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: And, pray, what made you forget it?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: The sun.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: The sun! He's mad. You mean the moon, I believe.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Oh, my dear Sir, you don't know the effect of a fine Spring morning upon a young fellow just arrived from Russia. The day look'd bright; trees budding; birds singing; the park was gay; so, egad, I took a hop, step, and a jump, out of your old balcony; made your deer fly before me like the wind; and chased them all round the park, to get an appetite, while you were snoring in bed, uncle.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Ah! so, the effect of English sun, upon a young Russian, is to make him jump out of a balcony, and worry my deer.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I confess it had that influence upon me.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: You had better be influenced by a rich old uncle; unless you think the sun likely to leave you a fat legacy.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Sir, I hate fat legacies.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Sir, that's mighty singular. They are pretty solid tokens of kindness, at least.

sp.speaker: Fred
sp.p: Very melancholy tokens, uncle—They are the posthumous despatches Affection sends to Gratitude, to inform us we have lost a generous friend.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: How charmingly the dog argues!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: But, I own my spirits ran away with me, this morning. I will obey you better in future; for they tell me you are a very worthy, good sort of old gentleman.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Now, who had the familiar impudence to tell you that?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Old Rusty, there.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Why, Humphrey, you didn't?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Yes, but I did, tho'.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Yes, he did; and, on that score I shall be anxious to shew you obedience: for, 'tis as meritorious to attempt sharing in a good man's heart, as it is paltry to have designs upon a rich man's money. A noble nature aims its attentions full breast high, uncle; a mean mind levels its dirty assiduities at the pocket.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Jump out of every window I have in my house! Hunt my deer into high fevers, my fine fellow! ay, damn it! this is spunk, and plain speaking! Give me a man, who is always plumping his dissent to my doctrines smack in my teeth.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I disagree with you there, uncle.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: So do I.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: You! you forward puppy! If you were not so old, I'd knock you down.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I'll knock you down, if you do. I won't have my servants thump'd into dumb flattery. I won't let you teach 'em to make Silence a toad-eater.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Come, you're ruffled—Let's go to the business of the morning.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Damn the business of the morning! Don't you see we are engaged in discussion? I hate the business of the morning.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: No, you don't.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: And why not?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Because 'tis Charity.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Pshaw! damn it—! well—we mustn't neglect business—If there be any distresses in the parish, read the morning list, Humphrey.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Jonathan Huggins, of Muck Mead, is put into prison.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Why, 'twas but last week Gripe, the attorney, recover'd two cottages for him, by law, worth sixty pounds.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: And charged a hundred and ten, for his trouble:—So, seized the cottages, for part of his bill, and threw Jonathan in jail, for the remainder.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: A harpy! I must relieve the poor fellow's distress.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: And I must kick his attorney.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: The Curate's horse is dead.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Pshaw! there's no distress in that.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Yes, there is—to a man who must go twenty miles, every Sunday, to preach three sermons, for thirty pounds a year.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Why won't Punmock, the vicar, give him another nag?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Because 'tis cheaper to get another curate, ready mounted.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: What's the name of the black pad I purchased, last Tuesday, at Tunbridge?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Belzebub.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Send Belzebub to the Curate, and tell him to work him, as long as he lives.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: And, if you have a tumble-down tit, send him to the vicar, to give him a chance of breaking his neck.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: What else?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Somewhat out of the common. There's one Lieutenant Worthington, a disabled officer, and a widower, come to lodge at Farmer Harrowby's, in the village. He's plaguy poor indeed, it seems; but more proud than poor, and more honest than proud.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: That sounds like a noble character!

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: And so, he sends to me for assistance?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: He'd see you hang'd first. Harrowby says, he'd sooner die than ask any man for a shilling. There's his daughter, and his dead wife's aunt, and an old corporal, that has served in the wars with him—he keeps them all upon his half-pay.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Starves them all, I am afraid, Humphrey.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Uncle, good morning!

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Where the devil are you running, now?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: To talk to Lieutenant Worthington.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: And, what may you be going to say to him?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I can't tell till I encounter him; and then, uncle, when I have an old gentleman by the hand, who is disabled in his country's service, and struggling to support his motherless child, a poor relation, and a faithful servant, in honourable indigence, —impulse will supply me with words, to express my sentiments.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Stop, you rogue! I must be before you, in this business.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: That depends upon who can run fastest. So, start fair, uncle! and here goes!

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Stop! Why, Frederick!—A jackanapes! —To take my department out of my hands! I'll disinherit the dog for his assurance.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: No, you won't.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Won't I? dam'me, if I—But we'll argue that point as we go. Come along, Humphrey!

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Corporal Foss crossing the Stage, Stephen following him.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Hollo! I say, Mr. Corporal!

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Ah! Master Stephen! is it you?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: What do you think I ha' been about?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Getting the cart and horses out of the mud, I suppose.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
Foss.
sp.p: A Pioneer is our name for it, my honest lad. Aye, I have seen some of that work, in my day, master Stephen! If we could get but a little spot of ground, now, with a bit of a good-for-nothing building upon it—

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: I ha' found out just such a pleace, Mr. Corporal.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Then I'll shew you the whole process.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: I ha' done the whole progress, myself.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Have you?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: You do know feyther's pig-stye?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Yes;—it stands on the edge of the dry ditch, at the back of the house.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: That's where it did use to stand, sure enow—But I ha' blow'd it up wi' gunpowder.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: The devil you have! and how?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: All according to rule, mun;—just as you laid it down. I bored a hole under the ditch, wi' the peel of our oven; and then I laid in my bumbustibles.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Why, I clapt the kitchen poker to un, red hot; and it all went, up wi' a desperate complosion, just as you destroy'd that outlandish buttery.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Bless us, master Stephen! then you have ruin'd the town, in cold blood, and kill'd all the inhabitants.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: No; the inhabitants am lying in the ditch, as pert as daisies—only the little pigs am singed quite bald, and the ould white sow be as black as the devil.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: Brother Stephen! Come here, brother Stephen. Feyther do vow vengeance again ye. If you do go on o' this fashion, what will the neighbours call ye, Stephen?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Call me? why, a perspiring young hero, of five foot six inches, willing to mortalize himself, in the field of March.

div.stage: Worthington crosses the stage, and goes into the house.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: There—his honour is come home—I must go in for orders.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: Oh, Mr. Corporal, Joe Shambles, the butcher's boy, ha' brought this from our town, for your master.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: One letter. Is this all he left for us, my pretty maid?

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: No; he left a leg of mutton.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: How stately Mr. Corporal do march, surely! he be as upright as our gander. Come, Mary! afore feyther do come home, lets you and I go wash the gunpowder pigs.

sp.speaker: Mary.
sp.p: How, Stephen?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: We'll go to the dairy, and chuck 'em into the milk pails.

sp.speaker: (Voice without.)
sp.p: Stephen!

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Wauns! there be feyther! Run, Mary, run!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Where are the ladies, Corporal?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: They are gone to take a walk, an' please your honour.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Oh.—
—Mine has somewhat fatigued me.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Under favour, I think your honour takes too much exercise—it always brings on the torment in your wound again.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: You bustle about for me, more than I could wish, Corporal. You got your wound in an ugly place, you know.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: I got it at Gibraltar; the same ugly place with your honour—That cursed shell struck us both together.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I remember it did, Corporal.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: And, when I lay on the ground, and your honour's left-arm was so terribly wounded, you stretch'd out your right, to help me.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I don't remember that, Corporal.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Don't you? but I do—and I wish I may be damn'd if ever I forget it.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Well, well—do not let us swear about it, Corporal.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: I hate swearing, your honour, as much as our Chaplain loved brandy; but when a man's heart's too full, I fancy, somehow, there's an oath at the top on't; and when that pops out, he's easy. Ah! we had warm work that day, your honour!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: We had, indeed, Corporal.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: There was Crillon's batteries, and four thousand men behind us at land.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Moreno, with his Fleet, before us at sea.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: At ten, in the morning, the Spanish Admiral began his cannonade.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Our battery from the King's bastion open'd directly.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Red-hot shot poured from the garrison.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Cannons roar!

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Mortars and howitzers!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: The enemy's shipping in flames!

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Fire again!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: They burn!

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: They blow up!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: They sink!

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Victory! Old England for ever, your honour! Huzza!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Aye, Corporal; against the world in arms, Old England for ever!

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: Huzza!

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: We have no limbs to help our country, now. We shall never fight for Old England again, your honour.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: No, Corporal; 'tis impossible!

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: But our hearts are for our country still. Tho' your honour has only half-pay, and I am but an out-pensioner of Chelsea.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: We have no right to complain, Corporal. National bounty, beyond its limits, would be national waste; and 'tis impossible to provide sumptuously for all.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: That's true, your honour. Every hero, that loses his life, in the field, must not expect a marvel monument.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: 'Tis of little import, Corporal—A gallant Soldier's memory will flourish, though humble turf be offer-bound upon his grave. The tears of his Country will moisten it; and vigorous laurel sprout among the cypress that shadows his remains. But 'tis a bitter thought, when we must depart, to leave, unprotected, the few who are joined with us, in the ties of affection, and the bonds of nature!

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Your honour is join'd in no bond with any body, but Mr. Burford, for five hundred pounds.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I did not mean that, Corporal. There, however, I am easy. My friend has strict honour: and, should he die, the regular insurance of his life secures me from injury, in lending him my name. But 'tis strange I have not heard from him.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: I had forgot—Here is a letter just brought for your honour.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Let me see—
“Tunbridge” —'Tis written in the neighbouring town—who should know me there?

“Sir,”“I am instructed by Mr. Ferret, solicitor of London, to inform you, that Mr. Burford died on the 26th ultimo, on his way to the Insurance office; whereby the Policy, which had expired the day before, is become void, and the Bond, and Warrant of attorney for 500l. remain in force against you. If the money be not paid, forthwith, I shall enter up judgment, instantly, for the recovery of the same.”My child! my child!

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Your honour!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Ruin'd past hope!

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Don't say that, your honour; for, while your half-pay continues—

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: My creditor will grasp all—My person seized, and my poor child destitute!

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Destitute! what, my young mistress?—and you?—and—don't give way to grief, your honour. I am lame, to be sure, but I am fit for labour still—There's my little pension, too, from Chelsea —Things may come about; and till they do, you and my young mistress shall never know want, while the old Corporal has a limb left to work, or a penny in his pocket.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Corporal, I—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Yes, this is he! Zounds! I am quite out of breath—Sir, I am come to—Whew! I beg pardon—but, as you perceive, I am devilishly blown.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Leave us, Corporal.
At your leisure, Sir, I shall be glad to know whom I have the honour of addressing.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I am Frederick Bramble, Sir. My uncle, Sir Robert Bramble, lives at the foot of this infernal hill. He fix'd his house there, I fancy, for the sake of argument; because most men maintain it is bad to build in a bottom. He is as charitable as a Christian, Sir, and as rich as a Jew.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I give you joy of a relation, Sir, who has so much virtue, with so much wealth. When Fortune enriches the benevolent, the Goddess removes the bandage from her brow, that she may bestow a gift with her eyes open. But as I am a stranger here, and a recluse, I have no right to enter further into your uncle's character.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Yet he has just now, Sir, taken a right to enter into yours.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: May he not rather have taken a liberty, Sir?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: 'Tis his duty to be the most inquisitive fellow in the neighbourhood.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: 'Tis a strange duty for a gentleman!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I hope not, in this country, Sir. If a gentleman be in the commission of the peace, and living on his own estate, he should be anxious, I think, to inquire into the conduct of those around him, that he may distribute justice as a magistrate, and kindness as a man.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: But how can your uncle's principle apply to me, Sir? A secluded sojourner, with a quiet family, lodging with one of his tenants?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Why, he has heard of the—hem!— that is, I mean—the—peculiarity of your situation—

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Sir!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I shall make a bungling business of this, after all!
—I say, Sir, that my uncle, as I told you, is a warm old heart, who busies himself in learning the circumstances of every body about him, and—

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: The circumstances!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Yes; and so Humphrey Dobbins,—a stupid old servant,—among other intelligence this morning, happened to—to mention you, and— damn it, Sir, the truth's the truth:—I ran here to prevent my uncle's offering his assistance too bluntly, and I fear I have done it too bluntly, myself.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: It wou'd be absurd, Sir, to affect blindness to the motives of your visit—I see them clearly, and thank you cordially. You have touch'd the heart of a veteran soldier; but go no further; if you proceed, you will wound the dignity of a gentleman.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I came here to heal wounds; by my soul I did! 'Tis not in my nature to inflict them. I am new in England; ignorant of the manners of the country—for I arrived here, last night, from Russia, where I was born; but surely, surely, it cannot be offensive, in any part of the globe, to tell the afflicted we feel for them. Pray, give me your hand!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Take it, Sir, take it. Receive the grasp of gratitude, and be gone.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Not till you first permit me to—

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I can accept no favours, of the nature you offer, where I have no claim: and what claim, young man, can I have upon your attentions?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: The claim each man has, in common, upon his fellow. We are all passengers on life's highway; and when a traveller sticks in the mire, on the road, the next that comes by is a brute who doesn't stretch out a hand, to extricate him.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: That may hold in the courtesies of life; but I do not admit it as an argument in essentials.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Then, I wish my uncle were here, with all my heart, Sir; he'd argue this point with you, or any other, to all eternity.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I want no arguments upon points of honour. Honour, the offspring of honesty, dictates for itself.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Sir, I respect it, for its parent's sake; tho' the child is a little maddish: for Honour is, sometimes, cutting throats, where Honesty would be shaking hands. But let me intreat you to relax—to be persuaded. Come, my dear Sir! true honour, I trust, can never have reason to blush, because honesty is assisted.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: You have burst upon me at a critical, a trying moment. I have a family; a beloved child, from whom I may be shortly torn, without the means of—No matter. Even the griefs that, inwardly, wring me, would not force me to unbend, were there not a native ingenuousness in your manner, which wins me. To you, then, to a youthful stranger, whose sympathy comes o'er a rugged soldier's nature, as pictured Love bestrides the lion, to you I will owe a temporary obligation.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Will you? Then, you have made me the happiest dog that—
Eh? —no—zounds—! I mean, Sir, you have made me look like the silliest dog in the world!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: In my haste to do service, I never, once recollected I wanted the means. My heart was so full, that I quite forgot my pockets were empty.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I cannot think, young man, you came here to insult me.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Insult! Oh, my dear Sir, you do not know me! You may soon. I have left a father, in embarrassments, in Russia. I have landed here, dependant on an uncle's bounty; and paid my last shilling, yesterday, to the coachman, who set me down at his gate; but my relation is as generous as a prince! he will, I am sure, give me a supply; and then—

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: And, then, I would not, for worlds, draw upon your little store. You have a superior call, it seems, upon you; a parent in distress.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: My father's involvements, no doubt, will be his brother's care; and if—

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: No more, no more! I see the workings of your heart. Farewell! You have sensibly affected me, and I must leave you. Repine not that your will to do good actions outruns your power. Had the widow been without her mite, and simply dropt a tear for Poverty, on the moist shrine of Compassion, it would have secured to her a page in Heaven's register.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Now, this is all very pretty rhodomontade; and I'll go, directly, and argue that it is so, with my uncle, for the good of this bluff veteran. A widow, weeping for distress, may water the road, pleasantly enough, for herself, to Paradise;—but if she could shed peck-loaves, instead of tears, it would be twenty times better for the poor's box.

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: Enter Sir Charles Cropland and Ollapod.

sp.speaker: Sir Charles.
sp.p: I'm as chilly as a bottle of Port, in a hard frost—This is your English Spring; that our shivering poets celebrate by a fire-side, if they can get one, and sing of basking shepherds, making love in the sun.—I'm as amorous as an Arcadian, but it's cursed cold, in Kent, for all that. Are you sure these women will come, Ollapod?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Sure as death, as I tell my patients.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: They find that, sure enough.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: He! he! Yes, Sir Charles; I never deceive them—Call'd in, last week, to Captain Custard, of our Corps, who was shovell'd off by a surfeit. “Dearest friend,” says I, looking in his fat face, “be firm”—Candour compels me to say, now I'm come, you can't live:” he didn't.— “You shall be buried with military honours”— he was. Attended him from beginning to end— doctor and mourner—Bed and grave—Physick'd him first, shot over him afterwards. Poor fellow! a good officer, an excellent pastry-cook, a prodigious eater, and a profitable patient!

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Damn Captain Custard! I am thinking of a fine girl, and you are panegyrising a dead pastry-cook. These women will disappoint us, at last.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Then there's no honour in the honourable Miss MacTab.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: You didn't see Emily?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Pshaw! all is uncertainty. I shall lose the golden fruit, at last.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Damn'd hard, after I've given the dragon a dose—Do you take, good Sir? do you take?

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: I wish the dragon had wings, then, to move a little faster. This sharp north-easterly wind will prevent their walking.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: I hope not, Sir Charles;—for they'll get a cursed cold, and want an apothecary.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Stay.—I think I see a petticoat.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Mark! 'tis an old bird—The honourable Miss MacTab, in a jog-trot.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: And Emily with her, by all that's beautiful!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Yes, that's she—As fine a woman as ever smelt sal-volatile. There's the game, Sir Charles. You've nothing to do but to kill.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Step aside, or our meeting will be too abrupt. We must kill by rule here, Ollapod.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Kill by rule? With all my heart! 'Tis a method I've long been used to.

div.stage: Enter Miss Lucretia MacTab, and Emily Worthington.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Cold? ridiculous! Females of fashion, Miss Emily, never complain of the cold, now.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: I didn't know it was the fashion to be insensible, grand-aunt.

sp.speaker: Luc.
Emily.
sp.p: Dear! that's a charming park yonder! Who can it belong to?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Sir Charles Cropland.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Sir Charles Cropland! Pray, let us get home again!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Does a fine country frighten you, Miss Emily?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: It used, in Canada.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: For what reason, pray?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Because a brute, sometimes, inhabits it.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Ridiculous! Should we happen to meet Sir Charles, I beg that—

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: What, is he here, then?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: So Mr. Ollapod informs me.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: And who is he?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: The apothe—Hem! the officer who visited the family, this morning.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: We will have no more walks, without my father, madam.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Oh, as you please; but—Eh! I declare here they both come—'Tis impossible to avoid them now.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Bless me!—This is very strange!

div.stage: [Sir Charles Cropland and Ollapod appear at the back of the scene.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Engage the old Tabby in talk; and move off with her, if you can.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Mum!—I'll bother her.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
