sp.p: Ladies, I am rejoiced to see you. To meet you in this part of the world, is, indeed, an unexpected pleasure.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: We are come here, you see, to rusticate. Sir Charles, as my poor dear brother, Lord Lofty, used to say.—Been vegetating here, for a week, at a wretched farm-house; but air is the grand article with me.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: At your dinner it is, I'll be sworn.
And what is your grand object, in the country, Miss Worthington?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: To be alone, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Umph! a strange propensity, permit me to say, for one so young, and so beautiful.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: I learn'd it from my father, Sir; we neither of us like intruders.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: That's a damn'd dowse in the blubberchops of my friend, the baronet.—I must talk to the old one—Hem! rural walks here, Ma'am— All green, and twisting, like a snake in a bottle of spirits.—Wood-pigeons in plenty.—Hear 'em cooing? Pop 'em down, here, by dozens.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: They are pleasing birds enough, in a grove, Sir.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: And pretty picking in a pye, Ma'am.
Yes —he's beginning—Must have Miss MacTab off soon.
Fond of views, Ma'am? Hill, dale, steeples, rivers, tufts of trees, and the like?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I admire a rich landscape, Sir. When my brother, the Baron, was planting clumps round Ricketty Castle, I used to say he was placing beauty-spots on the face of nature.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Did you? Come, that was very well, very well, indeed! Thank you, good Madam—I owe you one. Pretty sporting country to the right.
sp.stage: (She turns towards Sir Charles and Emily. He pulls her by the elbow.)
sp.p: That's to the left, Ma'am.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Bless me! this is a very rude man! Do you know, Sir Charles, that Emily has lost your beautiful little present?

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: What, the terrier puppy, from Leicestershire?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Gone—though he was in the apartment, when you last did us the honour of a call.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Unkind to set so little store by my present, Miss Worthington! and when did you observe the puppy was gone?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: The very moment you left the room, Sir.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Humph! that's another dowse for the baronet! I must get the old woman away!
Ma'am—!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Lord, Sir!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Condescend to cast your eye over that hillock —the little lump to the left there—round and black, like a Bolus. From that point, you see three capital counties at once.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I can't say that I perceive—

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Stay—here's Kent—Fertile in pheasants, cherries, hops, yeomen, codlings, and cricketters— On one side, Sussex—

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: In what beauties does that abound, Sir?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Mutton and dumplings.—And there's Surrey—Sweet Surrey!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: For what may that be famous?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Nothing that I know of, except my cousin, Crushjaws of Carshalton, who tugs out a stump with perfect pleasure to the patient.

div.stage: [During the above, Lucretia is continually endeavouring to turn towards Sir Charles, and Emily; and Ollapod, constantly, prevents her.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I protest I see nothing before me, but a barn.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: That's reckon'd the only eye-sore in the view; for it totally blocks out the prospect—Fifty yards further we may see all—A little swampy here, to be sure—Better for snipe shooting. Permit me to touch the tip of your honourable little finger, and pass you over the puddles.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Bless me! I can never get over that stile!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: A little gummy in the legs, I suppose.
Its the easiest in England, upon the honour of a Cornet—If an ankle's exposed, I'll forfeit all the physick in my shop. This way.
Step out there, Ma'am. Curse 'em! the cows have been here. This way!

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Gone! Permit me to follow my relation, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Stay, my dear Miss Worthington; I have something of the utmost consequence to say to you.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Speak it quickly, then, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Your father does not abound in riches, I take it.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: That is of no consequence to me, Sir, if he can be happy.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Now, I am very rich, as men of fashion go—for, my estate is not yet dipp'd above three parts of its value.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: That can be of no consequence to me at all, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Pardon me—for I have to propose to you—

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: What, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Your own house in town, the run of my estate in the country, your own chariot, two footmen, and six hundred a-year—But you must allow me a little time to myself—A little play at Miles's—a little sport at Newmarket—a little hunting in Leicestershire; and, this apart, you'll find me the most domestick man in the world.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: I fancy I comprehend the nature of your jargon, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Jargon! It is a language perfectly understood, by all us young fellows, in the circle of St. James's. 'Tis the way of the world, my dear little Simplicity!

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Oh! how base must be the world, then, when it makes simplicity its victim! I have been bred in wilds; but the sweet breath of Nature has inspired my soul with reason; common to every human bosom, as the wintry blasts, that roar'd above me, on the mountains. What does that reason tell me, Sir?—That vice is vice, however Society may polish it; that seduction is still seduction, however Fashion may sanction it; that intellect, speaking through simplicity, like mine, has the force of virtue to strengthen it; while worldly sophistry must shrink from native Truth, when it proclaims, that he, who could break a father's heart, by heaping splendid infamy upon his child, is a villain.—Let me pass you, Sir!

div.stage: Enter Frederick at the back of the scene.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I have lost my way, and my uncle, and— eh! who have we here?

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Upon my soul, you must not go.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: How, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Look ye, my dear Emily—I am advanced too far in the game to recede. If you are not mine by intreaty, there are four spanking greys, ready harness'd, in Cropland Park, here, that shall whisk us to town in a minute.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: You dare not, sure—

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Nay, faith, I dare any thing now—for, the prize is in my reach, and I will clasp it, though your heart were colder to me than the snows of Russia.
sp.stage: (He runs towards her, she screams— Frederick advances.)

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I bring news from that country, Sir—I arrived last night.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Then, Sir, you arrived damn'd mal à pros. What are you?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: A man—so, I am bound to protect females from brutality. You, it seems, assault them. Pray, Sir, what are you?

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: A person of some figure here, Sir. You may not know, perhaps, the consequence of insulting one of that description, in this country.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Faith, not I: but I know the consequence of his persisting to persecute a woman, in my presence.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: What may that be?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I knock him down.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: You will please to recollect, Sir, I am a gentleman.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I can't for the soul of me—I can never recollect that any man is a gentleman, when I find him forgetting it himself.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Can you fight, Sir?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Like a game cock, Sir—try me.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: What is your weapon, Sir?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: The Knout.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: What the devil's that?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: A Russian cat o'-nine-tails, to chastise a criminal; and I know no criminal who more richly deserves it than he who degrades manhood, by offering violence to the amiable sex, which nature form'd him to defend. Fear nothing, madam.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: We must meet again, my hot spark.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I'm happy to hear it—It implies you are going now.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Hark ye, Sir—I am call'd Sir Charles Cropland. Yonder is my park.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: With four spanking greys in it. I heard you say so.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: There is very retired shooting, in some parts of it, Sir—Your name.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Frederick Bramble;—nephew to your neighbour, Sir Robert. You'll find me ready to take a morning's sport with you.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: You shall hear from me. This is a cursed business!—but it will keep up the noise of my name at the Clubs; and the duel of a dashing Baronet furnishes food for the newspapers.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Victory, madam! The enemy is fled, and virtue triumphs in the field. Ha! you look pale!

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: I have been sadly flurried.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: 'Sdeath! she is near fainting!—Let me support you, madam.
Zouns! how beautiful she is! Tears! now would I give the world to kiss them off, and then kick the scoundrel that caused them.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: I know not how to thank you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I'm glad of it, ma'am—I never like to be thank'd for merely doing my duty.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: I fear, Sir, that—I mean, I hope that —I—I hope, Sir, you will not be exposed to further danger, on my account.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I am not used to think of danger, madam, on any account; but, something tells me, I shou'd glory in any that I risk'd for you. Whither shall I have the honour of attending you safe home, madam?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: I have a relation, Sir—a female relation, who has been walking with me: she is now, I fancy, in the next field, and she will—

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: What, an elderly lady, that I observed, just now, as I pass'd, with an officer?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Aye—that officer!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Who is he pray?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: A wicked accessary, I am convinced, of Sir Charles Cropland's!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Is he? I see him coming—huzza! I'll blow him to the devil, if he were generalissimo.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: For heaven's sake! you make me tremble.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Tremble! I woudn't give you pain for worlds! I'll be calm with him—On your account I will. I'll affront him with all the civility imaginable.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: The honourable Miss MacTab has tumbled up to her middle in the mud. Bless me, is Sir Charles gone?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: You are Sir Charles's friend, it seems, Sir?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: I have the honour to be close in his confidence.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: And assist him upon honorable occasions. You are an officer, I perceive.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: He! he! yes, Sir—Cornet in our volunteer Corps of Cavalry; as respectable a body as any regulars in christendom.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I don't doubt it at all. To stand forward at home, and keep off invaders from the shores of our country, is as honourable, and praise-worthy, as marching to attack its enemies abroad. Pray, don't be alarm'd—you see I'm civil.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: A pretty spoken young man—I'll encourage him. Come, that's very well—very well indeed! Thank you, good Sir—I owe you one.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: But some morbid parts may be found, I fancy, in the wholesomest bodies.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Decidedly.—Like a chubby child, in high health, with a whitlow.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Just such a whitlow I take you to be.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Me!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Exactly: and 'tis that uniform alone—as I respect every symbol of loyalty and patriotism,— that prevents my cropping your ears, as close as your jacket. Don't be uneasy, you see I'm civil.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Crop! Zounds! what do you mean?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Can't you take my meaning, in your own way?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Way! Sir, I engage to kill the enemies of my country, in the way of war,—I never draw blood from the natives, but in the way of business.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Business!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Yes; I'm an apothecary—Take care how you meddle with a man of my repute. Served my time, seven years, under old Cataplasm, of Canterbury; —took out my freedom in that ancient city; —thump'd the mortar, six months, at Maidstone;— now, on my own bottom, in trade, at Tunbridge. Cornet Ollapod, at the gilt Galen's-head; known to all the nobility round—Sharp shot in a copse— deep dab at the broad sword exercise—Charge a furze-bush, wing a wood-cock, or blister a lord, with any chap in the county. Insult me, as an officer, and I'll prosecute you—Touch my ears, you touch my honour, and, dam'me, I'll clap you in the county jail, for assaulting a freeman.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: That scarlet apothecary is beneath my notice: but if the fellow has flurried your nerves, Madam, which it is his trade to tranquillize, I'll pound him to death, in his own mortar.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Pray, do not be so violent:—It terrifies me—On your own account, Sir, it terrifies me.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: On my own account?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Yes. It would grieve me to see one, who is capable of such kind actions towards me, hurried into peril, by the warmth of his temper.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I will be what you please. Tell me only whither I shall lead you. You are of the neighbourhood, I conjecture. May I ask your name?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Emily Worthington, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Worthington! then you are daughter to the finest spirited man I ever met in my life.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Do you think so? Do you, indeed! I am very glad that you think so. But how came you acquainted?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Why, I—I had a little business with him;—but, somehow or other, I—I went without my credentials. Shall I take you to him? Will you trust yourself with me?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Trust myself! Oh yes! My dear father shall thank you. I will thank you; and our poor old Corporal, who has served in the wars, and follow'd us through America, he will thank you, in tears of joy, when he hears of this rescue.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: That old Corporal loves you then?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Certainly he does. He nursed me when my poor mother died, and left me an infant in Gibraltar; and dearly I love him, too.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Now, what would I give to be an old corporal!

I attend you—Let me see you home. Oh! how would it diminish the number of scoundrels in the world, if they could once taste the joy of rescuing a lovely female from perdition, and restoring her to her father!

div.head: SCENE II.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Emily not yet return'd—I cannot rest in this suspence—Every instant, I dread the arrival of these officers, to drag me from my family, from my child!—Ha! two strangers lurking yonder! Nay, then, I know their errand—Where is my Emily? Well, well, 'tis better, in such a struggle, if the child witness not the anguish of the parent.

div.stage: Enter Sir Robert Bramble and Humphrey Dobbins.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: So—here we are at last—That hill's a breather. I am sure that was my nephew I saw, hopping over the plough'd land, yonder.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Not a morsel like him.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I wonder if the rogue has found his way here yet. Ha—There's our man,—leaning against the stump of the tree, there. He seems lost in thought—Go, and tap him on the shoulder, Humphrey.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: You're wanted.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I understand you.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Your servant, Sir—Your name is Worthington, they tell me.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: It is, friend.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I have a little business with you; and it isn't my way to use ceremony.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I expect none, from a person of your stamp.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Stamp!—Humphrey, isn't that odd?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Not a bit.—The neighbours tell every body what a rum jockey you are.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Umph! you'll excuse me for talking before old Crabbed here—He's in all my affairs— The puppy has grown grey with me, and I can't well do without him.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Your follower, I suppose.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Yes, he's always at my heels. You have served his Majesty, I hear, and done your duty nobly.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: No matter.—Do your duty, and 'tis enough.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Yes, he's as proud as Lucifer, I see— but there's no flattery in that.
The motives that brought me here, will prove, I trust, that I don't always neglect my duty.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: You may perform it now, then—If my life depended on it, friend, I could not give you five pounds, at this moment.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Give me five pounds! Who the devil wishes you? I want to know how I can do you a kindness.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I thank you.—In consideration, then, for a gentleman, and in reliance on his honour to acknowledge the obligation, when in his power, I trust you will place me in an apartment in your own house.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: An apartment in my own house!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Yes—where I may have the comfort of privacy, and my family about me.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Damn me, but that is pretty plump, for a man who would sooner see me hang'd than ask me a favour!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: You will not, I think, be harsh enough to lodge me among the wretched rabble, who are the common inmates of your gloomy walls.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: My gloomy walls! an infernal, impudent old scoundrel! Squeezes himself, and all his relations, into my house, and calls my family a wretched rabble.
Humphrey, did you ever see such brass?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: I always told you, except myself, you kept but a queer set.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Zounds, I'll—No, I'll keep my temper. Pray, Sir, what can you suppose I am to make of you?

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Make of me!—These mercenary harpies! I have already told you, friend, you can make nothing of me, in my present situation—What you think you may make of me, in future, as a man of honour, I leave to your own feelings.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I won't consult my own feelings now, Sir;—I must proceed upon my judgment.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I know you are proceeding upon a Judgment.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: And that judgment is cursedly against you, at this moment, let me tell you.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: 'Tis my misfortune.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: If you think that a misfortune, you might as well alter your conduct with me a little. I don't see the drift on't.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Drift!

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Aye; where's the policy?

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: That expired but a few hours too soon.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: His policy expired but a few hours too soon! Why, the man's a maniac! His distresses have deranged him. Were you—hem—were you ever wounded in the head?

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Truce with interrogations, friend. I am ready to accompany you.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: You are! And, pray, where are we to go?

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I told you I should give your own house the preference.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Curse me if you ever shall set your foot over my threshold!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Lead me where you please, then. You profer'd kindness, and I was weak enough to expect it. But I might have known that one of your cast is deaf to the petition of distress.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: The devil I am!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Familiar with scenes of want, habit hardens your heart, till the very face becomes an index of the mind; and callous inhumanity scowls in every lineament of the hard-featured bailiff.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Blood and thunder! Bailiff! Humphrey, do I look a bit like a bailiff?

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: I don't know but you do.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Sir—I—pardon your mistake, and I like your spirit—There no flattery in it. But I'm in a passion for all that. Many a modern Sir Jacky looks like a prize-fighter; but its rather hard to take a baronet of the old school for a bumbailiff.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: My daughter!

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: And my sky-rocket of a nephew!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Ha! you are here at last, I perceive, uncle.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Uncle! Is this Sir Robert Bramble, then? the generous relation, of whom you told me?

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Generous! Psha! But I am his uncle; —though the puppy's smart enough, he is nephew to the hard-featured fellow, whose face is an index of his mind.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Oh, Sir, if you are his relation, talk to him, I intreat you—argue with him—

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Argue with him! that I will, with all my heart and soul! On what subject?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: On his rash intention, Sir, to meet the ruffian from whom he has just rescued me.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Rescued you, Emily! What does this mean?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Oh—a mere trifle—nothing—A gentleman, in the fields, here, happen'd to be so very civil to Miss Worthington, that I took it for rudeness —so, I happen'd to be so rude to him, that he cou'd'nt take it for civility, that's all.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Rudeness to my child! Who has dared to—But, come in, Emily—Your pardon, Sir,
You have found nothing but confusion here, and I must retire with my daughter, for an explanation. Come, Emily.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Let us thank this gentleman, before we go, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Upon my soul, I deserve no thanks, Sir. If I deserve any thing, Miss Worthington's good opinion more than repays me.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: To you, Sir Robert, I owe some apologies, for—

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I hate apologies, Sir—they look like flattery—'Twas a mistake—Will you, and your family, dine with me to-day?

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: If possible, we will attend you; but my time, now, depends upon contingencies. Come, Emily.

sp.speaker: Emily
sp.p: Farewell, Sir!—And, pray, pray be cautious.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Frederick,—who is the fellow you have been quarrelling with?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: He calls himself Sir Charles Cropland.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I know him.—He's a puppy—must you fight him?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: So he tells me.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I'll be your second.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: You!

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Yes—; fighting's a sort of sharp argument; and, as we defend the cause of insulted innocence, it's damn'd hard if we haven't the best on't. But hark ye, you dog—don't fall in love with the girl.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I have—

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: You hav'n't!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Over head and ears.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Why, you blockhead, she's a beggar.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: So am I—We shall make a very pretty couple.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: And, if you married, how would you support her?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Perhaps, you wou'd support us.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: You sha'n't have a shilling, till my death.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Then I hope we shall have the pleasure of starving together, a great while, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Run back, and order a dinner for a party. Tell old Buncles, the butler, to lug out some claret.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Then, after dinner, I'll drink Emily Worthington in a pint bumper.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Humphrey, you haven't attended, now, to a word of what was passing.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: Every syllable on't.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: You'll laugh to see me out in a duel, I suppose.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: No, I sha'n't—I'd sooner be shot at myself.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Umph! If my nephew marries this girl, I've a great mind to cut him off with a shilling.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: No you won't.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Why, you know he's as poor as a rat.

sp.speaker: Dob.
sp.p: The rat's your relation—It wou'd be plaguy hard to starve him, when you feed all the rest of the rats, in the parish.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Come along, Humphrey—And if ever you starve, rank bacon, and mouldy pye-crust, be my portion!

An aukward errand I'm on, to Sir Robert Bramble's. Not quite correct to carry a challenge into a family I've physick'd. But honour, in this case, before medicine: a leaf of laurel's worth twenty drops of laudanum. Mars is first customer, and damn Æsculapius! Ha! here comes the enemy, up hill, from the house! The game meets me half way, as Death does the doctor.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: “A pointed pain pierced deep my heart.” “A swift cold trembling seized on every part.”

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: That's an ague.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: “But quickly to my cost I found,” “'Twas love, not death, had made the wound.”

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Damn that disease! it's cured without an apothecary.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I've order'd dinner for my old uncle; and now, can't I, for my life, help loitering about the farm-house. What mind she has in every look! I would rather be a whale, and flounce about the Baltick, than fall in love with a fine proportion'd face of beautiful insipidity—'Tis a lamp without oil— Heaven in a fog—Give me those dear bewitching features, where sweet expression always speaks, and sometimes sparkles. Give me a dimpled beauty that—Zouns! here's that damn'd ugly apothecary! Pray, Sir, do you know what are some men's antipathies?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Yes; cats, rats, old maids, double-tripe, spiders, cheshire-cheese, and cork-cutters.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Now, my antipathy, Sir, is a pert apothecary. How dare you look me again in the face, without trembling?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Trembling! at what?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Death!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Pooh! I've made it my business to look Death in the face for fifteen years, and don't tremble at it at all.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Why do you presume, Sir, to come across me here?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Here! this is the King's highway—trod on as common as camomile—crowded with all comers, like the Red Cow on a field day. Besides, I've business at Blackberry Hall.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: At my uncle's?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Yes; I've something in my pocket to deliver there. You may guess what it is.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Lip-salve for the maid, perhaps; or rosewater, to put into puddings.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Damn lips, and puddings! I've a letter for you.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: You have!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Yes; to be taken directly.
Eh? isn't that Sir Robert Bramble?

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I've sprained my back, trying to frisk over that infernal farmer's hog-trough. If Humphrey hadn't argued I was too stiff in the joints to jump, I'd have seen the dog at the devil before I attempted it. Ha—Mr. Ollapod—Your servant —Your servant—Tell me what brings you this way?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: I'll see you in a fever first.

Dry weather for walking, Sir Robert—but no news.— Young partridges look'd for every day—so are six Hamburgh mails—Glad to find our gout is gone, Sir Robert—Happy to meet you again on a good footing. Do you take, good Sir? do you take?

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I take your jokes, as I do your bottles of physick, Master Ollapod.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: How is that, Sir Robert?

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I never take them at all.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Come, that's very well, very well, indeed! Thank you, good Sir, I owe you one.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Frederick! what are you doing here?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Reading a challenge, uncle.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: So!—'tis come then.—Who brought it?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Pestle and mortar there. Read, uncle, read!

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: “Sir,”“Mr. Ollapod, of the Volunteer Corps, will deliver this to you. You will find me, half an hour hence, at the plantation on the heath, waiting to receive the satisfaction due to”“Charles Cropland.”Plain as a demonstration in Euclid.—
But how dare you, who have bled my coachman, till he can't drive, and julep'd my cook, till she faints at a fire, administer a challenge to my nephew?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Honour is rigid, Sir Robert, and must be minded as strictly as a milk diet.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: You come here, in short, as Sir Charles Cropland's friend?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: I do. Gallipots must give way to gallant feelings,—and Galen is gagg'd by Bellona. Sorry to offend the Bramble Family. Shall bring lint, probe, and styptick, along with the pistols. Though serving as second, on one side, shall be proud to extract a ball for either party, on as reasonable terms as any in the profession.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I have been thinking, uncle, and—you sha'n't accompany me in this business.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I sha'n't! You puppy, hav'n't I a right to smell powder, if I please?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: 'Tis an awkward business, altogether,— perhaps a foolish one. I am a useless fellow, floating through the world like a mere feather. If I am blown out of sight, 'tis no matter. You are of too much value, uncle, to be made the sport of every idle gale.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Now, what, in the devil's name, is the value of a man, if he don't stand by his friend, when he wants him?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: And, what, in the devil's name, uncle, is the value of his friend, if he only drags him into a scrape?

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: A scrape!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Yes—. They tell me the law of this country is apt to call killing a man, in a duel, murder; and to look on all accessaries as principals. Now, uncle, as I am going on an expedition which may end in hanging, I don't think it quite considerate to inveigle an honest friend to be of the party.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I never heard the argument put in that way before. There are few, I fancy, of your opinion.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Oh, a great many. There are men enough to be found, who would give in the same opinion, by Twelve at a time. But shou'd I fall, in my encounter, with this booby of a baronet—

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Fall!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Why, 'twould be bold to argue, uncle, if a bullet hits in a mortal place, that it won't kill— and, in case of the worst, I have a request to make—

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: If I fall, then, uncle, you—You know I have a father.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Well!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: He is your brother, my dear uncle! An affectionate brother. Your tempers may not assimilate, but he loves you—He is poor
—If I fall, remember him.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: My dear, dear Frederick! your death would break my heart—I have been reasoning all my life, and find that all argument will vanish before one touch of nature.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: I fancy you will often find it so, my dear uncle.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: And nature tells me, if you argue for ages, you sha'n't prevent the old man's going with you. Come, we must go home to prepare—You must have my pistols, and—upon my soul, Frederick, I love my brother Job—We'll have him over, and—zounds! this will all end in smoke —and then I'll write to Russia—We'll have a family party, and be jolly, and—Come, my dear lad, come!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: This young man may rashly plunge into a quarrel on Emily's account. 'Tis my duty to chastise the insulter of my child. At Sir Robert Bramble's I might learn more, and—but, in what a state of mind should I attend him!
So, Corporal! have you observed any people about the house?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: No enemies, your honour; unless they are in ambuscade.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I am strongly inclined to go to Sir Robert's to-day.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: I hope your honour will. They say he is such a good-hearted old gentleman—Ten to one but he gives your honour a helping hand.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Then he'll think I come to solicit assistance! I will not go.

sp.speaker: Foss
sp.p: Won't you, your honour?

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I wish to see my daughter again, Corporal.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: I had almost made sure of your honour's going—I have laid out the red roquelaure; and, in case of a dark night, Stephen's now in the stable, dusting out the lantern, for me, to march home before your honour.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Well, well,—send Emily to me—

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Heigho! Oh, here comes my young lady!
Make him go to Sir Robert's, Miss Emily—Bless you, do!—Mollify his honour a bit.—You don't know half the good may come on't—Do now!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: What said the Corporal, Emily?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: He bid me press our going to Sir Robert Bramble's to-day.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Should you wish me, Emily, to place myself in a situation where I might be suspected of imploring support?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Heaven forbid! But the gentleman, who protected me, has been so good,—so very good,— that—

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: That what, Emily?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: I—should like to thank him—that's all.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Have we not both thanked him, already?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Yes—but—not enough, perhaps.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: If more be necessary, I may express our further sense of his goodness by letter.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: The service he did me was not by letter, you know, my dear father.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: You seem strangely interested here, Emily!

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Shouldn't I be so! I hope I ought: for indeed, indeed—I—I am very uneasy.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: My child!—uneasy!—compose yourself, Emily.—Open your heart to me; to your father; your friend, Emily!

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Indeed, I never wish to hide my thoughts from you. They often meet your ear, so wild, and so unform'd, that they resemble dreams.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Alas, my child! the thoughts of young minds too frequently resemble dreams;—dawning dreams of happiness, my Emily, which vanish as our day opens. Should you love this young man, Emily, it is a dream from which no reproof of mine shall startle you; but the gentleness of a father shall awaken you.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Love him! Oh, no:—but, he preserved me from danger, and, on that account, I dread he may incur it himself.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: You know not, yet, what your heart is, Emily.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Yes, indeed, I do.—I should be grieved if I did not know it dearly loved you.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: And you have no such sentiments towards this young man, Emily?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: No, upon my word. The sentiments I feel for him are as different as light and darkness.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: My dearest Emily, till you know the world's path better, be cautious how you tread. Lovely blossoms open ere the fruit is form'd, and the heart expands, before the judgment ripens. I may soon be snatch'd from you, Emily—

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: My father!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Disappointment, too, may press on the heel of Age, and hasten his step with me to the grave.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: My dearest father!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Take, then, my fondest counsel while I live—my best legacy, alas! should I be hurried from you. Act not too suddenly on ideas. Doubt that passion may mislead you, till reflection justifies your impulse. Wed not for wealth, Emily, without love; 'tis gaudy slavery;—nor for love without competence; 'tis twofold misery. Go not against the current of your station nor deserts—. Glide gently down the stream, with neither too full a sail, nor too slight a freightage, and may your voyage, my child, be happier—much happier than your father's!

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Madam MacTab wants to know if you all dine at Sir Robert's, your honour.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Why does she inquire, corporal?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: It's about putting on some of her trinkums, and furbelows, I fancy, your honour. She came in, a while ago, as muddy as our little pigeon-toed drummer, after a long march.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I have thought on't—Tell her we shall go.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: No! Will you? Huzza! I ha'n't been better pleased since they made me a Corporal.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: You will go, then?

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Some explanation is necessary there, and I will make up my mind to bury other feelings. I might hesitate, perhaps, in taking you with me, but you have heard my counsel, and I know my child. Lucretia will go with us—We must, afterwards, take our leave of her entirely.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Indeed!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Her conduct, of which you have inform'd me, with Sir Charles Cropland, has decided me; and she will only quit a tottering asylum. I have to tell you our friend Burford is dead, Emily.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: What! the friend that—

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Yes, Emily—A worthy, an honourable man—but from the suddenness of his death—'tis fit I prepare you for the shock—he has left me in involvements, which, in a few hours, may inclose me in a prison.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: A prison!—You!—You will take me with you—Won't you take me with you?

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Like the eagle on the rock, Emily, I must shelter my nestling where Providence ordains.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Well, then, do not make yourself unhappy, my dear father! We shall not be very miserable, if we are not asunder.—I will sit by you— talk to you—listen to you—and, should a tear steal upon your cheek, I can kiss it off, and—
I am not shock'd for myself—pray, forgive me!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: My beloved, my amiable child!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: If we live here for a twelvemonth, I'll never speak to that beastly quack, who left me in a ditch, again.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: We shall not live here for a twelvemonth, Madam; and after what has pass'd, you will feel as little surprise, as I mean offence, when I propose to you to relinquish the fortunes of a man, whose situation, in all places, must be so irksome to you.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I—I understand—You are weak enough, then, Mr. Worthington, to wish me to withdraw my countenance from the family.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Since the strength of your zeal for my family, Madam, has so far outrun my weak notions of its happiness, I confess I do wish you to withdraw it!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: 'Tis very well, Sir!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: When you are ready, Madam, to go to Sir Robert Bramble's, you will find Emily, and me, in the garden, prepared to attend you. Come, my love!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Then the Honourable Miss Lucretia MacTab is cut, at last, by a half-pay Lieutenant, in a marching regiment.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Is your ladyship's honour ready to go?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Go! are you sent to drum me out, fellow, as you would a deserter?

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: I don't come to drum your ladyship's honour; —I want to know if you'll go to Sir Robert's.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Go, to-morrow, by break of day, to the post-house. Ask if there's a return chaise there, for London.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: What am I to do then, an' it please you?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Secure a seat in it, for the Honourable Miss Lucretia MacTab.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Is your ladyship's honour bundling off, then?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Bundling, you brute! obey my orders.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: That I will, with all my heart and soul, an' please your honour!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I'll withdraw myself from this wretched family —I'll go down to Scotland, and patronise my sixteenth cousin, the tobacconist of Glasgow.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Here be the lantern, Master Corporal. I have made him shine like our barn door. If you do like a duck, now, for your supper, I ha' shot one of ourn for you, wi' father's blunderbuss.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: How came you to do that, my honest lad?

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Why, she ware a marching before a whole brood of young ones—and look'd, for all the world, like a captain at the head of his attachment. We have no herbs to stuff her, for I ha' cut up all our kitchen garden, to look like a mortification.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Well, well—I must attend his honour—But keep a sharp look out, my good lad!—You know what I told you.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: What, about the bum-baileys? rot um! I'll blow 'em up wi' gunpowder.

sp.speaker: Foss.
sp.p: Keep a good watch, that's all.

sp.speaker: Stephen.
sp.p: Dang me, if a soldier's hurt on our premises. I've unmuzzled Towzer and Cabbage; they'll bite all as come, good or bad. Come you along, Mr. Corporal.

div.head: SCENE the last.
div.stage: Enter Sir Charles Cropland and Ollapod.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: We are on the ground first.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Perhaps the enemy's subject to a common complaint.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Troubled with a palpitation of heart, and can't come.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: He doesn't seem of that sort. What are the odds now, that he doesn't wing me? These greenhorns generally hit every thing but the man they aim at.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Do they! zounds! then the odds are that he'll wing me—I'll be principal, if you please;— for, to say the truth, I never served my time to the trade of a second.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Psha! you must measure the distance, when he comes, Ollapod.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: What's the usual distance, Sir Charles?

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Eight paces.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Bless me! men might as well fight across a counter. Does the second always measure the ground?

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: 'Tis the custom.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Then you had better have chosen one a little longer in the legs. If I was to fight, I'd come out with a Colossus.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: I see him coming to the style.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: There! he has jumped over. Curse him! he's as nimble as quicksilver—And there's old Sir Robert, waddling behind him, like a badger.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: They are here.

div.stage: Enter Sir Robert Bramble and Frederick.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Gently, Frederick! I tell you I'm out of breath.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: We shall be too late, and—Oh! here's my man. I hope we hav'n't kept you waiting, Sir. They say, in England, when people are to shoot at one another, it's the only engagement in which it's the fashion to be punctual.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: You are pretty exact, Sir.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Let us lose no time, if you please, then;— for dinner will be spoil'd.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Perhaps, Sir, one of us may never go to dinner again.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: No; but my uncle will—and 'twould be a pity he should have his meat over-roasted.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Mr. Ollapod, be so good as to walk over the ground.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Left foot foremost, as they do in the Infantry?

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Hold, Sir Charles! Perhaps this matter may be brought to an accommodation.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: I don't well see how, Sir Robert.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: If you are alive to fair argument, I think I shall convince you you have been cursedly in the wrong.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: I didn't come here to argue, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Didn't you! Frederick, you must shoot him. A man that won't listen to argument deserves to be blown to the devil.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Five, six, seven, eight.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: We'll take our ground if you please, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Give me that, Ollapod; and success to hair-triggers!

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Here is your pistol, my dear lad.— Zounds! my heart is as heavy as a bullet! Happen what will, I shall never forget poor Job; and as for you, Frederick—Come, damn it, we mustn't blubber, now.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Stop—here's somebody coming—Medical man never witness'd a finer crisis!

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: My friend! Sir Robert Bramble, too! pistols!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Stand out of the way, my dear Sir! Whoever is on his legs, after the first fire, will have the pleasure of speaking to you.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Stay, gentlemen! This business, I believe, requires my interference.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: And pray, Sir, what may make your interference so necessary?

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I conceive you to be Sir Charles Cropland; —which argues—

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Don't waste your arguments: they'll be all thrown away upon him.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: I am Sir Charles Cropland, Sir; and, pray, who are you?

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I will tell you, Sir.—I am a man, into whose family a serpent has basely crept, to corrupt my child; but her mind is fraught with too much sense, and virtue, to fall beneath his wiles; and, ruffian-like, he has attempted force to complete his purposes. I am an officer, Sir, in his Majesty's army—quick to resent a private injury, as I have been ready to face my country's foes. I am one, Sir, who am as gratified to meet you, that I may chastise you, as you merit,—as you have ever been industrious to skulk from me, conscious of the punishment you have deserved. I need not tell you my name is Worthington.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Dam'me, but that is better than argument; and as unlike flattery as any thing I ever heard in my life!

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Now, pray, Sir, are you and I to go home to our dinners, or are we to swallow a forced-meat ball in the fields?

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: We had better suspend the business, Sir—There are ladies coming.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Your father has trotted on, child, as if he was on a forced march. Bless me!
who have we here?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: My father—with Sir Robert, and— ha! Sir Charles Cropland there!

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: And that brute who left me in the mire.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: That's me.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: You and I, Sir Charles, must find another moment for explanation.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: The immediate moment may be the best, Mr. Worthington. I believe I may have been so fashionable in my ideas, that they may have led me wrong; and I don't think it a very bad style, though it mayn't be modern, to confess it.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: The style of sense and honesty, Sir, must ever meet approbation; that of folly, contempt; that of offence, correction; and, I shou'd be sorry if the style of repentance did not find forgiveness.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Or the style of argument, listeners.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: Miss Worthington, I confess my fault, and plead for pardon. You will not only, I hope, afford me your own, but intercede with Mr. Worthington for his, also. You check'd me—

rather roughly indeed—in a career which I have acknowledged to be wrong, Sir.—Instead, therefore, of proceeding in resentment, it will be better to offer you my thanks, if you will be pleased to accept them.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Sir, 'tis pleasanter to be thank'd than shot at, any time; and I accept them willingly.

sp.speaker: Sir Cha.
sp.p: I take my leave then. I hav'n't dash'd thro' this scrape according to present principles— a man's owning he is sorry for his vices may get him laugh'd at, among a few gay friends, who have more spirits than thought; but I believe he'll hunt the pleasanter for it, in Leicestershire.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Miss Lucretia MacTab, I confess my fault, and plead for pardon, since I, unluckily, left you in a puddle; and I sincerely hope you'll never be in such a pickle again.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Stand away, you brute!

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Sir Robert, I hope you won't withdraw your friendship—and it would give me a mortification to be cut off from your custom.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Oh, master Ollapod, your little foibles are like your small quantities of magnesia; they give no great nausea, and do neither harm nor good.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: Come, that's very well, very well indeed! Thank you, good Sir, I owe you one—I'll stay, and he'll ask me to dinner.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob
sp.p: And, what are you saying, there, to Miss Worthington, Frederick.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Telling her what good cheer there is in Blackberry Hall, uncle—and what a worthy gentleman at the head of the table, where I am going to have the pleasure to lead her.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: You are devilish ready to do the honours; —isn't he, Mr. Worthington?

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: To do honour to the human heart, Sir, I have found him very ready.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: And have you found him so very ready to do honour to the heart, Miss Worthington?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Yes, indeed I have, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I begin to perceive it. I'm a strange old fellow—fond of argument, they say. But I have so little time left, now, in this world, that some of my arguments are a little shorter than they used to be. When I was hobbling over the stile, after Frederick, there,—and thought the dog might be shivered to atoms—I made a determination in my own mind, if he happen'd to survive, that he, and your daughter—What's your name, young lady?

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: Emily, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Ha! a pretty name enough—that he and Emily shou'd make a happy couple.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Never, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: That's a plump negatur. We'll argue that point, if you please.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: My child, Sir Robert, has heard my opinions very lately; and hearing the opinions of a friend, she adopts them.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Does she? Then she's as little like Humphrey Dobbins in her mind, as she is in her features.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: To you it may, now, be necessary to say that I am poorer even than poor—but observe, I disdain all solicitations—This very day I have been apprised—

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Oh, I know what you mean—The bond for five hundred pounds.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: How came you apprised of that bond, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I have paid it.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: Paid it!

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Yes—while Frederick was loading his pistols, in the next room, to come to the field, here.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: You astonish me!

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Why so? I happen to be Sheriff of the County; and, as all writs are returnable to me, a scrubbyish fellow ask'd me to sign one against you. I thought it might be as well not to lock up a worthy man, in a scurvy room, just as I had ask'd him, from no common motives, to sit down to my table—so, I drew upon my bankers, instead of John Doe, and Richard Roe,—and you may reimburse me at your leisure.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: My dear, dear uncle! you have been before me here!

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: You rogue, if your fortune could serve you as well as your legs, I believe you'd have been before me here, too.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I know not what to say to you, Sir Robert.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Confess you're a damn'd bad physiognomist, and I'm content. Say a man's countenance may a little belye his nature;—though, as Sheriff of the County, I own I am head of the bum-bailiffs.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I shall never be able to repay you this debt, Sir, but by long, and miserable instalments.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: You shall give me security.

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: I wish it. Any in my power.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Miss Emily, pray come here—Frederick, you dog, come on the other side of me. Let me appoint you two trustees for a bond Mr. Worthington shall give me—a bond of family alliance —fulfil your charge punctually, and Heaven prosper you in your obligations. Mr. Worthington, what say you?

sp.speaker: Worth.
sp.p: You overwhelm me—I cannot speak.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: The trustees are dumb too:—but I see they are embracing the obligations, pretty willingly.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: A marriage between the young ones. I hope I may be in favour with the family, nine months hence.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Sir Robert, I rejoice at the alliance. The Brambles came in with the Conqueror, and are no disgrace to the MacTabs.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: I haven't the honor to know exactly, who you may be, Madam; but I thank you. But, damn it!—our dinner will be waiting.—Make one of the party, if you please, Ollapod.

sp.speaker: Olla.
sp.p: I'll attack your mutton with all my heart, Sir Robert. I knew he'd ask me to dinner.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: Come, Emily! let me lead you to a house, where our days may be long, be happy. You look doubtingly.

sp.speaker: Emily.
sp.p: No, indeed—When my father doubted, I have doubted—but I can read his eyes—as he, I own, not long since, read my heart. You have been my preserver, and I can't help feeling gratitude.

sp.speaker: Sir Rob.
sp.p: Love, you mean, you little devil! Frederick, we'll have Job a grandfather before he can get from Russia.

sp.speaker: Fred.
sp.p: My dear uncle, your hand—Mr. Worthington, suffer me to press yours. Emily, you have my heart. And may hearts, when unvitiated by the world, meet the happiness I expect, and the approbation of the Virtuous!
